chunks: Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said:

I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: A man trims his nails, cuts his moustache, and takes from the hair of his beard and his head—does that invalidate his wudu (ablution)? He said: O Zurārah, all of this is sunnah (prophetic tradition), and wudu (ablution) is an obligation. Nothing from the sunnah (prophetic tradition) invalidates the obligation, and indeed that surely increases him in purification.

key_terms.تَطْهِيرًا: purification, indicating an increase in cleanliness and purity
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: a sunnah (prophetic tradition), meaning a recommended normative practice
key_terms.فَرِيضَةٌ: an obligation, referring here to wudu (ablution) as a required ritual state
key_terms.وُضُوءَهُ: his wudu (ablution), the ritual state of purification in question
key_terms.يَنْقُضُ: invalidates or breaks, meaning nullifies ritual purity

ai.seo_question: Do cutting nails or trimming hair invalidate wudu (ablution) in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith explains that trimming the nails, shortening the moustache, and taking hair from the beard and head do not invalidate wudu (ablution). The Imam عليه السلام distinguishes between sunnah (prophetic tradition) acts of grooming and the obligatory state of wudu (ablution), affirming that such grooming only adds to cleanliness and purification.
